claims.text: The initial equiatomic FeNiCrMn alloy is a single-phase FCC crystal.
The initial FeNiCrMn crystal contains pre-existing chemical short-range order.
The initial FeNiCrMn crystal contains no vacancy clusters or HCP precipitates.
Shockley partial dislocations in FeNiCrMn nucleate in response to the local SRO energy landscape rather than at vacancy clusters.
The critical nucleation stress is determined by the crystallographic orientation's ability to sustain an SRO configuration that resists intrinsic stacking-fault formation.
Loading along <11-1> produces a higher maximum yield stress than loading along <110>.
The <11-1> orientation raises the yield stress because its slip-plane alignment maximizes the SRO-related energy barrier for Shockley-partial nucleation or glide.
The <110> orientation permits easier SRO disruption or lower local friction than <11-1>.
Partial-dislocation deformation creates intrinsic stacking faults that appear locally HCP-like.
The HCP-like regions are transient intrinsic stacking faults stabilized by local SRO rather than a true phase transformation.
A true FCC-to-HCP transformation has a significantly higher energy barrier than partial-dislocation nucleation at the simulated strain rates.
Bulk HCP transformation is suppressed by the high interfacial-energy cost of a true phase boundary.
At high-rate MD timescales, dislocation motion is fast relative to diffusion, so SRO can be treated as static during nucleation.
At lower strain rates, thermal activation and diffusion-driven SRO dynamics may alter the nucleation mechanism.
Yield strength in FeNiCrMn is relatively insensitive to strain rate from 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1.
Yield strength in FeNiCrMn decreases as temperature increases.
The <11-1> stress-strain curve will have a higher peak stress before the sudden stress drop associated with partial-dislocation nucleation.
A lack of a distinct phase boundary or bulk-HCP lattice-parameter shift would distinguish local stacking faults from a coherent HCP transformation.
The interaction between the <11-1> and <110> orientations and the SRO distribution in FeNiCrMn has not been explicitly quantified.
Introducing controlled vacancy clusters and recording whether partials nucleate preferentially at those sites can discriminate vacancy-mediated nucleation from SRO-mediated nucleation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes the higher barrier to the extra energy needed to disrupt local SRO, but cited record PMC8357793::rubric_gaps::013::85995a7fe4 reports that this SRO-breakup interpretation was contradicted by low-stress edge-dislocation motion in MoNbTaW.
